Q: Django Migrations: run_before vs dependencies A:

run_before is the exact opposite of dependencies. You should read it as "this migration must run before these other migrations".

Generally you should be using dependencies over run_before. One use-case where you need run_before is if an external app has a dependency in some way on one of your migrations.

This is also explained in "Controlling the order of migrations".

Q: How can different parts of a HTML Text node be formatted differently? A:

The formatting is coming from the font, not from the HTML or CSS splitting the text node.

The element contains only one text node:

<div class="ods-price__value">4.99*</div>

The site applies the custom LidlFontPricePublicBeta font to it. That font contains OpenType substitution rules that replace certain character sequences with alternative glyphs.

In particular, two digits following a decimal point are represented by smaller glyphs. So .99 is still ordinary text as far as the DOM is concerned; the font renderer simply selects different glyphs for those characters.

This is why removing the custom font makes the 9s appear at their normal size. It also explains why the behavior is specific to patterns such as .01–.99, without requiring separate <span> elements.

The effect is therefore encoded in the font's OpenType tables, most likely through contextual or ligature substitution.

Q: Why does YAML with colon inside quotes fail parsing? A:

The problem here is that in YAML, double quotes are only parsed as syntactic elements if they occur at the beginning of a scalar. Thus,

a:
  - "b c: "

would be valid YAML where the list item parses into the string b c: .

Now, the design of YAML has been driven by the goal to allow unquoted scalars whereever possible. Thus, it allows you to use double-quotes as content if they occur anywhere in the scalar after the initial character. Consequentially,

a:
  - b "c"

is valid YAML and the list item parses into the string a "b" where both double-quotes are simply part of the content. Since the scalar does not start with a double quote, it is an unquoted scalar, which means that even the double quote at the end is parsed as content.

Applying this to your input, we can see that the first quotation mark parses as content. Thus, the succeeding colon will be parsed as c-mapping-value, i.e. an indicator that starts a mapping value and implicitly assigns to the scalar in front of it the role of a mapping key.

The following example illustrates how this can be used to write valid YAML:

a:
  - b "c: foo

Now, the list item becomes a mapping that maps the key b "c to the value foo.

But in your code, there is another quotation mark after the colon. And this time, since it is syntactically located at the beginning of a scalar, it gets parsed as syntactic element. But since nothing follows it, you basically have written an unclosed scalar, which is a syntax error.

As for the question of why it works with "c:": The colon is only parsed as mapping value indicator if it is followed by whitespace. Thus, if you write

a:
  - b "c:"

the list item parses into the string b "c:".

So what to do? That depends on what you're trying to do. If you want a scalar that contains b "c: " as content, you can use any of the following scalar formats:

a:
  - "b \"c: \""
  - 'b "c: "'
  - |-
    b "c: "
  - >-
    b "c: "

If however you assume that your content works as implicit string concatenation (as it does for example on the bash command line) and want to get the string b c: , you would instead write

a:
  - "b c: "

This seems awfully complicated!

… yes. The following examples are not to defend the design, just to give you an understanding what it was supposed to do:

  • You can write URLs as plain scalars, e.g. http://example.com, because the colon is only syntax if followed by whitespace.
  • You can write command-line instructions as plain scalars, e.g. cd "Program Files", because the quotation marks are content if they don't occur at the beginning of the scalar.

Bonus content:

The colon does not need a space behind it if the key is given with quotation marks and the map uses the explicit flow notation with { ... }:

a: 
  - {"b":"c"}

But why?

Because YAML also wants to be a superset of JSON, i.e. all JSON should parse as YAML. Since JSON does not have this rule with a space after the colon, YAML also doesn't if the surrounding construct uses JSON notation (flow notation in YAML terms).

Q: Automation: how to automate transforming .doc to .docx? A:

A current option is msdoc2docx. It converts legacy .doc files to .docx using pure Python, without automating Microsoft Word, LibreOffice, or COM.

Install it with:

python -m pip install msdoc2docx

To convert every .doc file in a directory:

doc2docx batch input-directory -o output-directory --recursive --report batch.json

The --recursive option includes subdirectories and preserves their relative layout. The JSON report records successful and failed conversions, along with any unsupported or approximated content.

For a single file, you can use:

doc2docx input.doc -o output.docx

The converter does not yet support every legacy Word feature, so checking the generated report is recommended.

Disclosure: I am the author of this project.
